docs.title: 1. Executive summary
docs.text:
KNode is an AI-assisted platform intended to help African-focused nonprofit organisations discover relevant funding opportunities, present evidence of their capabilities, and identify organisations whose capabilities complement their own. It also supports funders who need to review organisations and proposed collectives against opportunity requirements. Its goal is to make funding discovery and collaboration more evidence-based, explainable, and accessible without replacing human judgement.

The product combines several layers:

  • Web frontend: the user-facing experience for account access and the organisation- and funder-facing workflows. The supplied hosted entry point is the sign-up page. Project context indicates a React/Next.js frontend; the frontend source was not part of the backend repository archive reviewed for this document.
  • Backend API: a FastAPI application that validates requests, applies business rules, coordinates feature services, enforces access controls where implemented, and returns data to the frontend.
  • Data layer: PostgreSQL is the configured target database. The product data model covers users, organisations, funders, opportunities, requirements, evidence, matching runs and results, collectives, referrals, workspaces, reports, and audit events.
  • AI and document intelligence: AI-assisted extraction and requirement assessment can structure information from funding calls and organisation documents. Results should remain traceable to source evidence and visibly distinguish known facts from generated or uncertain content.
  • Operational integrations: external AI providers, email delivery, and permitted public information sources support extraction, reporting, and discovery when configured and approved.

KNode should be understood as a decision-support platform, not an automated grant-award system. A match or partner suggestion does not confirm legal eligibility, organisational legitimacy, partner consent, or the likelihood of receiving funding.

docs.title: 2. Problem and product purpose
docs.text:
Organisations often have to search across multiple websites, reports, registries, and informal networks to find suitable funding. Funding calls are commonly written as long, unstructured documents, while evidence of an organisation's work can be spread across annual reports, project pages, financial filings, and other public material. Funders face the corresponding challenge of assessing organisations and combinations of organisations without having enough time to reconstruct the evidence manually.

KNode's core problem statement is:

Organisations struggle to match their capabilities with complementary partners to meet funding requirements, while funders struggle to assess the combined capabilities and track record of collaboratives.

The product is intended to help users answer questions such as:

  • What funding opportunities are relevant, and where did each opportunity come from?
  • What does a funding call require, including eligibility, geography, thematic priorities, deadlines, and partnership rules?
  • What evidence supports an organisation's profile and its ability to meet a requirement?
  • Which requirements appear met, partly met, unknown, or unsupported by the available evidence?
  • Which other organisations might complement a capability gap for a particular opportunity?
  • How could a proposed collective cover the opportunity's requirements, and what gaps remain?
  • What should a funder review before deciding whether to engage with an organisation or collective?

docs.title: 3.1 Primary users
docs.text: User group Main needs Intended product areas Organisation users (NGOs/NPOs) Maintain an evidence-backed profile, discover opportunities, understand gaps, and find potential complementary partners Organisation profile, opportunity discovery, matching results, partner suggestions, collective builder/workspace, reports, and trend/gap analysis Funder users Publish or review opportunities, assess organisations and proposed collectives, and refer relevant organisations Funder profile, opportunity management, organisation/collective discovery, evidence review, shortlists/referrals, and reports KNode administrators/reviewers Support platform operations, investigate flagged or uncertain records, and oversee access or quality processes Administrative and review workflows, audit-related records, and operational controls; the exact UI and permissions require implementation verification Collective members Coordinate contributions and responsibilities around a funding opportunity Collective membership, invitations, roles, tasks, notes, documents/links, requirement checklists, and gap tracking

docs.title: 3.2 Main product areas
docs.text:
1. Account access and profiles — account registration and authentication, organisation/funder profile information, and role-aware access.
  2. Opportunity intelligence and search — discover opportunities, preserve their source and verification state, and structure long calls into comparable requirements.
  3. Evidence profiles and evidence ledger — collect or upload source material, extract claims, preserve provenance and evidence status, and allow appropriate review/correction.
  4. Opportunity matching — compare opportunity requirements with available organisational evidence and show the reasoning and information gaps.
  5. Complementary organisation discovery — suggest potential partners based on capabilities, geography, programmes, and evidence gaps, not popularity or network size.
  6. Collective builder and workspace — assemble potential collaborators, understand collective-level coverage, and coordinate work for a shared opportunity.
  7. Funder discovery and referrals — help funders review relevant organisations or collectives and create referrals with clear status and context.
  8. Reports and notifications — deliver useful results and updates, including email reports when the relevant delivery integration is configured.
  9. Trend and gap analysis — present funding trends and identify information or capability gaps relevant to an organisation and an opportunity.

These areas describe the product scope from the requirements and data model. They do not imply that every screen or end-to-end workflow is currently complete in the deployed frontend.

docs.title: 4.1 Hosted entry point
docs.text:
The hosted frontend URL supplied for this document is:

  • KNode sign-up page

The URL identifies the sign-up route of the deployed frontend. Frontend source context available for this project also includes a KNode application shell with navigation entries for Dashboard, My Collectives, Trend Analysis, and Organisation Profile. These entries establish intended frontend areas, but a navigation link does not prove that the destination page is complete or connected to live data. The hosted page could not be fetched in the current review environment, so this document does not make claims about its current visual layout, exact fields, validation messages, or successful connection to the production API. Those details should be verified in a browser and against the current frontend source before being treated as confirmed behaviour.

docs.title: 4.2 Frontend responsibilities
docs.text:
At a solution level, the frontend is the interaction layer. It should:

  • present account registration and sign-in flows appropriate to user roles;
  • collect and validate user input before sending API requests;
  • display organisation/funder information, opportunities, evidence, matching results, and collective/referral workflows as those screens become available;
  • make evidence provenance, review status, unknown information, and AI-generated content understandable to users;
  • show loading, empty, success, validation, permission, and service-error states rather than treating every response as success;
  • respect the access decisions made by the backend and avoid relying on client-side role checks as the security boundary; and
  • use the KNode API rather than connecting directly to the database, AI model, or source-data providers.

docs.title: 5. End-to-end solution architecture
docs.text: KNode is designed as a web application backed by an API and a relational data store. The frontend should communicate with the backend API only. The API owns access checks, business rules, persistence, and coordination with AI and external services.

docs.title: 5.1 Frontend layer
docs.text: The frontend is responsible for the user-facing experience and API consumption. The deployed sign-up URL is known, but a complete screen inventory and verified API contract require review of the frontend repository and the running application.

docs.title: 5.2 Backend/API layer
docs.text:
The inspected backend uses Python and FastAPI. Its main responsibilities include:

  • exposing HTTP endpoints and OpenAPI documentation;
  • validating requests and response structures with Pydantic;
  • applying business logic and access checks through routers, dependencies, and services;
  • managing account and profile operations;
  • coordinating opportunity, evidence, matching, collective, referral, workspace, trend, and report functions; and
  • returning errors in API responses and recording operational information.

The implementation uses a layered structure with routers, schemas, services, repositories, SQLAlchemy models, and shared core/infrastructure modules. The separation is not absolute in every module, so this should be understood as the current repository convention rather than a claim of strict Clean Architecture.

docs.title: 5.3 Data layer
docs.text:
PostgreSQL is the configured target database for the backend. The data model defines persistent records for users, organisations, funders, sources, extracted claims, opportunities, requirements, matches and matching runs, collectives and their members, referrals, workspace items, reports, AI-related files/passages, and audit events. Alembic is used for schema migrations.

The data model specifies source traceability and explicit handling of unknown values. Missing information should remain missing or unknown rather than being filled with a guess. The deployed schema and migration state still need to be validated against the actual project database before the model document is treated as proof of production state.

docs.title: 5.4 AI and external services
docs.text:
The backend repository includes Google Gen AI/Gemini-related integrations for selected extraction and matching tasks. Provider availability depends on environment configuration. The code review found keyword-overlap retrieval in the matching path; the backend implementation inspected did not establish that vector search or pgvector retrieval was wired into that path. The separate backend technical document should remain the source for implementation-level detail.

The product requirements describe external data collection and email/report delivery as part of the intended system. Use of any external provider or public data source must respect access terms, privacy requirements, and approved configuration. A provider appearing in a requirements document is not proof that a production integration is enabled.

docs.title: 6. Core user workflows
docs.text: The following workflows summarize the intended product behaviour. Individual steps may be implemented to different levels and must be verified through frontend/API integration tests.

docs.title: 6.1 Registration and account access
docs.text:
1. A user opens the hosted sign-up page.
  2. The frontend collects registration information and submits it to the KNode API.
  3. The backend validates the request and handles account creation and authentication-related processes.
  4. The user is directed into the appropriate organisation or funder experience when the relevant frontend journey is implemented.

The backend contains authentication-related routes and services. The current hosted sign-up page's fields, validation behaviour, email verification experience, and successful post-sign-up journey were not independently verified in this pass.

docs.title: 6.2 Opportunity discovery and structuring
docs.text:
1. An opportunity is created, collected, or submitted from a permitted source.
  2. Its source/provenance and verification state are preserved.
  3. The opportunity content is converted into structured requirements such as geography, applicant type, thematic priorities, financial criteria, partnership conditions, and deadline where the source supports them.
  4. Unclear fields remain “Not specified” or another approved unknown state.
  5. Users review the opportunity and its source before relying on it.

The requirements emphasise that an aggregator-only opportunity must not be presented as verified without suitable confirmation and that a deadline must not be inferred when the source is ambiguous.

docs.title: 6.3 Evidence profile and review
docs.text:
1. Public-source information or an uploaded document enters the evidence-processing workflow.
  2. The system extracts candidate claims and retains a link to the source and relevant passage where available.
  3. Extracted claims are structured and assigned an appropriate evidence/review status.
  4. Organisation users review, correct, or remove extracted claims where the product workflow supports it.
  5. The displayed profile distinguishes source-backed information, organisation-supplied information, AI-generated suggestions, and unknowns.

Uploaded documents should not be publicly accessible by default. Visibility and sharing permissions must be enforced by the backend and verified before sensitive evidence is exposed to funders or partners.

docs.title: 6.4 Opportunity matching and gap analysis
docs.text:
1. The system identifies relevant opportunity requirements and available organisational evidence.
  2. Hard eligibility conditions, where implemented and supported by reliable data, are checked separately from evidence interpretation.
  3. Relevant evidence passages are retrieved and assessed against individual requirements.
  4. Results show the supporting evidence and explain gaps or uncertainty.
  5. The organisation uses the results to decide whether to investigate or pursue the opportunity.

A result is a decision-support signal. It does not prove eligibility or predict a funding award. Unknown or unavailable evidence must not automatically be interpreted as proof that the organisation lacks a capability.

docs.title: 6.5 Complementary partner discovery and collectives
docs.text:
1. An organisation identifies an opportunity or capability gap.
  2. KNode considers whether other organisations have evidence that could complement the gap.
  3. Suggested partners are presented as possibilities (for example, “may complement”), not as confirmed collaborators or definitive “best” partners.
  4. The user can evaluate and invite potential members.
  5. A collective-level view helps identify which requirements have evidence coverage and what remains unresolved.
  6. Members coordinate roles, contributions, tasks, documents, and notes in a shared workspace where those features are available.

The product requirements explicitly reject discovery ordering based on connection count, profile views, popularity, or network size. Complementarity should be grounded in capability, geography, programme experience, and evidence—not similarity alone.

docs.title: 6.6 Funder discovery, referrals, and reports
docs.text: Funders are intended to review organisations and potential collectives with supporting evidence, gaps, and unknowns; create referrals; and receive or send reports through the relevant delivery workflow. A referral is an introduction, not an endorsement or funding decision. Email delivery depends on configured and tested provider integration.

docs.title: 6.7 Trends and gap analysis
docs.text: The product requirements include trend analysis for funding opportunities and analysis of what an organisation needs to strengthen for an opportunity. The presence of trend-related backend modules does not establish that a complete dashboard visualization or end-to-end frontend workflow is deployed. The available data, aggregation logic, UI, and expected outputs need acceptance testing.

docs.title: 7. AI boundaries and evidence principles
docs.text:
AI is used to reduce the effort of structuring information and interpreting evidence. It must not become the sole authority for access, eligibility, evidence truth, partner consent, or funding decisions.

Key principles from the product and security requirements are:

  • Source traceability: important claims and assessments should link to their origin and retain retrieval or verification context where available.
  • Explicit uncertainty: missing, conflicting, outdated, blocked, and unassessed information should remain distinguishable.
  • Human review: organisations should be able to review relevant extracted claims; uncertain or high-impact information should be routed for appropriate review.
  • Separation of responsibilities: deterministic rules handle hard constraints and application permissions; AI helps extract or interpret text and draft explanations.
  • No invented facts: if a requirement or claim cannot be supported, it should be marked unknown or not specified instead of inferred.
  • No false assurance: a match does not confirm legal eligibility, legitimacy, willingness to collaborate, or likelihood of funding.
  • Fair discovery: connection counts, popularity, and network size must not determine which organisation is surfaced as a potential partner.
  • Visible AI provenance: AI-generated content must be distinguishable from organisation-confirmed or independently verified information.

docs.title: 8. Security, privacy, and governance
docs.text:
The Security and Privacy Requirements document sets expectations for authentication, least-privilege authorization, secure handling of personal and organisational data, safe document processing, source collection controls, logging, backup/recovery, incident handling, and security testing. These are requirements, not a certification that every control is currently implemented.

Areas the solution must address include:

  • role-based access for organisation users, funders, and administrators/reviewers;
  • object-level and tenant-level authorization, including prevention of insecure direct object reference (IDOR) access;
  • secure password storage and appropriately protected authentication tokens/cookies;
  • private-by-default uploaded documents and controlled field-level sharing;
  • secrets management and restricted access to external provider credentials;
  • validation and safe processing of uploaded documents;
  • server-side protections for any URL fetching or crawling, including SSRF controls, rate limiting, and robots.txt/terms compliance;
  • privacy-conscious logs, audit records for sensitive operations, and data minimisation;
  • encryption, backup, recovery, retention, and breach-response controls; and
  • security review and automated testing before deployment.

The backend source contains authentication/security utilities and access-control components, but implementation coverage must be assessed per route and workflow. This document does not claim that the system has passed a full security audit, achieved OWASP ASVS Level 2, or completed all privacy requirements.

docs.title: Status vocabulary
docs.text:
• Implemented in code: relevant code exists; this does not prove production readiness or acceptance.
  • Partially implemented: some parts exist, but integration, coverage, quality, or supporting infrastructure remains incomplete or unverified.
  • Planned / specified: described in the product or security requirements without sufficient implementation evidence in the reviewed source.
  • Not verified: evidence available in this documentation pass is insufficient to make a reliable claim.
  • Requires decision: product or technical sources conflict and an authorised owner must resolve the conflict.

docs.title: 11. Key limitations and open decisions
docs.text:
1. Frontend source and runtime validation: review the frontend repository, route inventory, API client, authentication state, environment variables, and actual deployed flows. The supplied signup URL could not be loaded during this pass.
  2. Scoring and ranking policy: reconcile the Product Requirements Document with the Epics before exposing numeric scores or ranked organisation labels.
  3. Requirement status vocabulary: agree the canonical labels for met, partially met, not met, unknown, not checked, and technical error, and map backend schemas to the approved user-facing terminology.
  4. Evidence review and visibility: verify that unreviewed claims and uploaded documents are not exposed beyond their permitted audience.
  5. AI and retrieval configuration: document the exact model/provider, credentials configuration, retrieval implementation, output validation, failure behaviour, and version tracking used in each environment.
  6. Database state: run and verify migrations against the target PostgreSQL database and test with the intended production driver.
  7. End-to-end workflows: test registration through to authenticated dashboard access, opportunity discovery, evidence review, matching, partner suggestions, collective workflows, referrals, and report delivery.
  8. Security readiness: perform route-level authorization testing, dependency and secret scanning, upload/SSRF testing where applicable, and deployment configuration review.
  9. Data source permissions: confirm the legal basis, licence terms, access restrictions, robots.txt behaviour, and refresh policy for each public or third-party source.

docs.title: 12. Recommended validation plan
docs.text:
Before describing the MVP as production-ready, validate the complete user journey rather than testing the API in isolation:

  1. Open the hosted sign-up page and verify layout, required fields, client-side validation, API errors, and success behaviour.
  2. Register and authenticate test organisation and funder accounts; confirm the correct role-specific landing experience.
  3. Verify that a user cannot access another organisation's private profile, evidence, documents, reports, or collective workspace by changing identifiers.
  4. Create or retrieve an opportunity and confirm that provenance, verification state, deadline, and unknown fields are shown accurately.
  5. Process representative documents and confirm every extracted claim links to its source and displays the correct review/visibility status.
  6. Run matching against representative evidence, including positive, partial, conflicting, missing, and technically failed cases. Confirm the result does not turn missing evidence into a negative fact.
  7. Test complementary partner suggestions for evidence relevance and ensure connection counts, popularity, and network size do not affect discovery.
  8. Test collective coverage and invitations, referral state changes, report generation, and email delivery with approved test accounts.
  9. Run backend tests against PostgreSQL as well as isolated test databases, and run frontend-to-backend integration tests against the deployed environment.
  10. Complete the security and privacy review required by the project's Security and Privacy Requirements document.

docs.title: 13. Glossary

docs.title: 1. Overview
docs.text:
The KNode backend is the application and data layer for a platform that helps African-focused organisations understand funding requirements, identify complementary partners, and organise collaboration around funding opportunities. It exposes JSON HTTP endpoints and coordinates authentication and authorisation, profile management, opportunity management, evidence processing, matching, collectives, referrals, workspaces, trend analysis, and external integrations.

The backend structures and surfaces evidence to support human decision-making. It does not decide funding outcomes, certify organisations, guarantee eligibility, or establish that a potential partner has agreed to participate. Missing information must remain distinguishable from negative evidence.

This document describes the backend's main components and points to the detailed references:

  • Database and Migrations
  • API Reference
  • Authentication and Security
  • Matching Engine
  • Testing and Operations

docs.title: 3. Backend architecture
docs.text:
The application uses a layered structure. Routers define HTTP endpoints, Pydantic schemas validate incoming and outgoing data, services implement business workflows, repositories encapsulate persistence queries, SQLAlchemy models define database entities, and core/infrastructure modules provide configuration, security, dependencies, logging, and error handling.

A typical request follows this path:

  1. FastAPI matches the HTTP request to a registered route.
  2. Pydantic validates path, query, and request-body values.
  3. Dependencies resolve the database session and, for protected routes, the current user.
  4. The router delegates business operations to a service.
  5. The service applies business rules, access checks, repository operations, and any required external-provider calls.
  6. Data is persisted through SQLAlchemy where applicable.
  7. A response schema shapes the returned result.
  8. Exception handlers and logging convert failures into client-safe responses and operational records.

Application wiring in main.py includes CORS configuration, correlation-ID middleware, error handlers, router registration, and the public /health endpoint.

docs.text:

docs.title: 5. Backend feature coverage
docs.text:
The backend supports multiple product areas; the Matching Engine is only one of them.

  • Authentication and user management: registration, verification, login, token refresh/logout, current-user access, password and OTP-related flows.
  • Organisation management: organisation profiles, team management, documents, and organisation evidence.
  • Funder management: funder profiles, funding interests and funder evidence.
  • Funding opportunities: opportunity creation, retrieval, update/deletion, extraction, and requirement management.
  • Evidence and claims: source records, extracted claims, review status and provenance.
  • Matching and partner discovery: requirement assessments, eligibility outputs, score/evidence summaries, and potential partner suggestions.
  • Collectives and coverage: collective records, membership, invitations/responses, coverage and lead suggestions.
  • Referrals: creation, retrieval, response and withdrawal workflows.
  • Workspaces: collective-associated workspaces and workspace items.
  • Trend analysis: analysis over available funding-related data.
  • Reports and audit: report-related data structures and audit-event services exist; the presence of these structures does not prove every report or audit workflow is exposed or complete.

For detailed endpoint paths, see the API Reference. For business logic and limitations of matching, see the Matching Engine.

core/config.py uses pydantic-settings, loads settings from .env, uses case-insensitive names, and ignores extra settings. database.py separately calls load_dotenv() and reads DATABASE_URL directly, so database setup and application settings have two access paths.

Important configuration names identified in the source include:

Variable Purpose / observed default DATABASE_URL Required database connection string. JWT_SECRET Required secret; minimum length is configured as 32 characters. Never commit it. CORS_ALLOW_ORIGINS Required allowed-origin configuration. APP_BASE_URL Required application base URL. ENV Environment such as dev, test, staging, or prod. DEBUG Debug flag; observed default true. Review before production. APP_NAME Observed default KNode. API_V1_PREFIX Observed default /api/v1; router prefixes are not fully uniform. JWT_ALGORITHM Observed default HS256. ACCESS_TOKEN_TTL_SECONDS Observed default 900 seconds. REFRESH_TOKEN_TTL_SECONDS Observed default 43200 seconds. OTP_TTL_SECONDS Observed default 600 seconds. OTP_LENGTH Observed default 6. OTP_MAX_ATTEMPTS Observed default 5. LOGIN_MAX_ATTEMPTS Observed default 5. LOGIN_LOCKOUT_SECONDS Observed default 900 seconds. PASSWORD_MIN_LENGTH Observed default 12. REFRESH_COOKIE_NAME Observed default knode_refresh. REFRESH_COOKIE_SECURE Observed default true; production transport should be verified. REFRESH_COOKIE_SAMESITE Observed default lax. REFRESH_COOKIE_DOMAIN Optional cookie domain. EMAIL_BACKEND Observed options include SMTP and Resend; verify the active implementation. SMTP_HOST, SMTP_PORT, SMTP_USER, SMTP_PASSWORD, SMTP_FROM_NAME Email delivery configuration. REFERRAL_DISCLAIMER_VERSION Observed default v1. GCP_PROJECT_ID, GCP_REGION Google Cloud / Vertex AI configuration; observed region africa-south1. GEMINI_TIMEOUT_SECONDS, GEMINI_MAX_RETRIES, AI_MAX_TEXT_LENGTH AI timeout, retry and text-size controls; observed defaults include 30 seconds, 2 retries and 20000 characters.

Never put actual credentials in documentation, examples, screenshots, logs, or version control. Use placeholders in examples and supply secrets through an appropriate local or deployment secret mechanism.

docs.title: 7. Startup and local development
docs.text:
The application entry point is main.py, and the FastAPI app is titled KNode, version 0.1.0. The public GET /health route returns {"status":"ok"}. FastAPI's default interactive documentation is available at /docs, and the OpenAPI schema at /openapi.json when enabled by the application.

The repository README documents these commands:

uv venv
uv pip install -r pyproject.toml --group dev
uv run --no-sync uvicorn main:app --reload

The commands should be verified in a clean environment before being treated as definitive. See Testing and Operations for the complete local setup and verification workflow.

docs.text:

Integration Code area Configuration / limitations Profile/opportunity extraction services/ai_service.py Uses GEMINI_API_KEY or a GCP project/region path depending on the module. External calls were not verified in a live environment. Document extraction services/document_extraction.py Defines ExtractionUnavailable (503) and ExtractionFailed (502). Review supported MIME types and conversion branches in code. Provider failures are translated to assessment errors. Email services/email_service.py SMTP configuration; uses STARTTLS. Missing credentials are treated differently in development and production. Treat source documents, web content, and extracted text as untrusted. Model output must not grant access, bypass backend validation, or write arbitrary database values. Preserve source and claim IDs, validate quotes against stored evidence, and avoid logging raw sensitive documents or secrets.

docs.title: 9. Background jobs
docs.text:
Relevant modules include services/jobs/opportunity_matching.py, process_grants.py, funder_crawler.py, midnight_grants.py, midnight_scraper.py, nightly.py, scraper.py, services/jobs/base.py, and services/matching_batch_service.py.

opportunity_matching.py provides a CLI entry point that opens a database session, runs run_opportunity_matching_batch, logs a summary, and exits through run_job. The batch service loads open opportunities and organisations, applies the configured provider policy, and iterates through candidates. A production scheduler/orchestrator was not verified in the inspected source.

Before running jobs in a shared environment, confirm the target database, job locks, failure recovery, provider-cost limits, retry behaviour, duplicate-execution safety, sensitive logging, and run-outcome recording.

docs.title: 10. Errors and observability
docs.text:
Pydantic and FastAPI handle request validation, services apply business checks, and database constraints provide an additional integrity boundary. The codebase contains both core/error_handlers.py and core/errors.py; main.py registration order may cause one AppError handler to replace another. Verify the effective handler and standardise the response contract.

Logging is configured in main.py through configure_logging, with DEBUG in development and INFO otherwise. Correlation-ID middleware is installed. The unhandled exception handler logs the exception and request path. The matching provider logs prompt version, attempt count, status, elapsed time and failure class rather than the raw prompt/evidence. The email service logs whether email was sent or skipped. Audit-event models and service modules exist, but complete audit coverage is not established.

Not verified: metrics backend, distributed tracing exporter, alerting, production log aggregation, database performance dashboard, complete sensitive-action audit coverage, or a database-readiness endpoint. /health returns a constant status object and is not a database-readiness check.

docs.title: 11. Deployment and operations
docs.text:
Before release:

  1. Build from a clean dependency resolution.
  2. Configure secrets through the deployment platform.
  3. Run Alembic migrations as a controlled release step.
  4. Verify the application start command and environment.
  5. Confirm /health responds after deployment.
  6. Smoke-test authentication, organisation/opportunity access and matching.
  7. Schedule batch jobs only if intended and ensure locks/retries are safe.
  8. Verify SMTP and AI credentials, network access, quotas and provider failure behaviour.
  9. Confirm backup/restore, log retention and incident-response procedures.

docs.title: 12. Developer maintenance
docs.text:
When adding an endpoint, use the existing router and prefix convention, define request/response schemas, keep business logic in services, enforce resource-level authorisation, add repository methods where appropriate, test success and failure paths, and confirm the route appears at the intended path in /openapi.json.

When changing a database field, update the SQLAlchemy model, create and review an Alembic migration, test it on disposable PostgreSQL, update schemas and service logic, and add persistence/API tests. Base.metadata.create_all() in tests is not a substitute for testing Alembic migrations.

For matching changes, define status semantics and evidence requirements first, keep provider access behind the assessment-provider interface, preserve claim/source IDs and quotes, validate provider output, keep eligibility separate from capability scoring, add labelled evaluation cases, record versions where supported, and verify authorisation before retrieving or returning organisation/collective information.

docs.title: 1. API conventions
docs.text:
The FastAPI application is identified as KNode version 0.1.0. For local development, the base URL is commonly http://127.0.0.1:8000. When enabled, interactive documentation is available at /docs and the generated OpenAPI document at /openapi.json.

docs.title: Create a match assessment
docs.text:
POST /api/v1/matches

  • Request schema: schemas.matching.MatchCreateRequest.
  • Response schema: MatchResponse.
  • Expected success status: 201 in the inspected route.
  • Service call: matching_service.create_match_assessment(db, user, organisation_id, opportunity_id, provider).
  • Persistence may create match_runs and matches records.
  • Invalid body or malformed UUID: typically 422.
  • Missing resources: not-found response.
  • Access violation: forbidden or not-found, depending on the path's disclosure policy.
  • Provider failures may appear in the assessment status rather than always failing the HTTP request.

Example body (confirm exact schema before use):

{
  "organisation_id": "<organisation-uuid>",
  "opportunity_id": "<opportunity-uuid>"
}

docs.title: List matches
docs.text:
GET /api/v1/matches

Query parameters identified in the source include organisation_id, opportunity_id, limit (1–100, default 20) and offset (minimum 0, default 0). Authentication is required. The response uses MatchListResponse and should filter results by the caller's permitted scope.

docs.title: Retrieve a match
docs.text:
GET /api/v1/matches/{match_id}

Returns MatchResponse. Access is resolved through _get_accessible_match; the inspected policy considers organisation management scope or a funder associated with the opportunity. A not-found response may be intentional to avoid disclosing that another tenant's resource exists.

docs.title: Partner suggestions
docs.text:
GET /api/v1/matches/{match_id}/partners

Returns PartnerSuggestionsResponse. The view logic looks for organisations with MET or PARTIALLY_MET assessments for requirements that remain gaps for the lead organisation. The response should say that a candidate may complement the lead; it must not imply availability, agreement or confirmed participation.

docs.title: 4. Errors and response contracts
docs.text:
Exact response formats vary because both core.errors and core.error_handlers register handlers. Capture real responses from the running application before treating the examples as definitive.

Typical categories include:

Situation Typical status Notes Missing, invalid or expired access token 401 Token/dependency validation. Insufficient role or resource scope 403 Permission check. Resource not found 404 Some paths use not-found to reduce resource-existence disclosure. Request validation error 422 FastAPI/Pydantic. Conflict 409 ConflictError, where used. Account lockout 423 AccountLockedError. Too many OTP attempts 429 OtpTooManyAttemptsError. AI extraction unavailable 503 ExtractionUnavailable. AI extraction failed 502 ExtractionFailed. A validation response may contain an error code, message and field-level details. Other responses may contain an HTTP-style code and correlation ID. Do not expose raw database errors, provider payloads, credentials or source document contents in client-facing errors.

docs.title: 1. Security overview
docs.text:
The backend uses token-based authentication and role/resource-scope checks. The main controls identified in the source include Argon2 password hashing, JWT expiry and token-type validation, token JTI revocation checks, inactive-account rejection, dependency helpers for role and organisation/funder scope, Pydantic validation, generic handling of unexpected errors, correlation-ID middleware, an audit-event model/service, and AI prompt/evidence-grounding safeguards.

The presence of a helper or model does not prove every route uses it correctly. Resource-level authorization must be verified route by route, including list endpoints, request-body identifiers, query parameters, uploads, evidence retrieval, and workspace access.

docs.title: Password hashing
docs.text: core/security.py uses Argon2's PasswordHasher with explicit parameters. The database stores a password hash, not a plaintext password. Never log passwords or verification codes. Confirm that password policy and hashing configuration are applied consistently across registration and password-reset flows.

docs.title: JWTs
docs.text:
The token helpers create JWTs with claims including:

  • sub: subject/user identifier.
  • type: token purpose, such as access, refresh, email verification or password reset.
  • iat: issued-at time.
  • exp: expiry time.
  • jti: random token identifier used by revocation checks.

JWT_SECRET and JWT_ALGORITHM configure signing/verification. The secret must be strong, private, and rotated through a controlled procedure. Do not commit secrets or include them in error messages, logs or documentation.

docs.title: OTPs and opaque tokens
docs.text: The code includes OTP generation and hashing using SHA-256 with constant-time comparison, along with opaque-token creation and hashing helpers. Settings include OTP lifetime, OTP length and maximum attempts, plus login attempt and lockout controls. Verify that attempt counters and revocation/OTP state are shared safely across multiple processes and survive restarts when required. In-memory state is not shared automatically between workers.

docs.title: 3. Authentication request flow
docs.text:
core/dependencies.py reads the bearer token, decodes an access token, handles invalid/expired tokens, checks JTI revocation and user revocation-after-issued-at, loads the user, and rejects missing or inactive accounts. Additional dependencies enforce roles and resource scopes.

The main helper categories are:

Helper Intended responsibility Review note get_current_user Resolve the authenticated user from the access token. Confirm consistent use on protected endpoints. require_role / require_any_role Restrict routes to specified roles. Role checks do not replace object-level authorization. require_organisation_scope Check organisation-related access. Verify the resource ID used is the one being accessed. require_funder_scope Check funder-related access. Verify cross-funder isolation. require_self_or_admin Intended to permit self-access or admin access. The inspected implementation returns the current user without comparing the supplied target user ID; it is not a reliable ownership check until fixed or guarded by a separate verified check.

docs.title: 4. Authorization requirements
docs.text:
Use both role-level and resource-level authorization. A valid token or correct role alone does not mean a user can access every organisation, funder, opportunity, match, collective, evidence source, referral or workspace.

Required verification includes:

  1. A user from one organisation cannot read or modify another organisation's private records.
  2. A funder cannot access unrelated funder data or match results outside its permitted scope.
  3. Resource identifiers in a body or query string cannot bypass access checks.
  4. List endpoints filter records by caller scope rather than returning broad database results.
  5. Evidence ledgers and uploaded documents are protected against cross-tenant access.
  6. Collective membership, invitations, referral targets and workspace items have appropriate access rules.
  7. Administrative privileges are explicit and tested.
  8. Sensitive routes return consistent 401/403/404 behaviour according to a deliberate disclosure policy.

Some routes may return 404 rather than 403 to avoid revealing that another tenant's resource exists. Document and test that behaviour rather than applying it inconsistently.

docs.title: 5. Cookies, CORS and production configuration
docs.text:
The observed settings include refresh-cookie name knode_refresh, REFRESH_COOKIE_SECURE=true, SameSite=lax, and an optional cookie domain. Verify the actual refresh-token transport and cookie attributes in the deployed configuration. Production must use HTTPS, appropriate secure-cookie settings, narrowly scoped CORS origins, and a strong secret managed outside source control.

The configuration includes CORS_ALLOW_ORIGINS, APP_BASE_URL, ENV, and DEBUG. Review production values explicitly; do not rely on development defaults. Ensure secrets are not accidentally included in logs or exception traces.

docs.title: 6. Evidence and AI safety
docs.text:
Treat source documents, web pages, extracted text, and model outputs as untrusted. AI output must not determine permissions, bypass service validation, or write arbitrary database fields. Preserve source/claim identifiers and verify cited quotations against the stored passage. Distinguish provider failure from unknown evidence and from a negative finding.

Before sending sensitive organisational material to an external AI provider, review the provider, region, retention, contractual and data-processing policies. Validate file type, size, storage location and access rules before upload, retrieval or AI submission. Avoid logging raw documents, credentials, tokens or full prompts containing sensitive evidence.

docs.title: 7. Error handling and information disclosure
docs.text:
The repository contains both core/error_handlers.py and core/errors.py. main.py registration order may cause one AppError handler to replace another. Verify which handler is effective and standardise error payloads and correlation IDs.

Client-facing errors should not expose raw database exceptions, SQL, provider payloads, secrets, or source-document contents. Unexpected exceptions should be logged with suitable context while returning a generic client-safe response. Do not include personal or sensitive data in correlation IDs.

docs.title: 8. Audit logging and operational security
docs.text:
The codebase contains an audit_events model and audit service/repository modules. This is not proof that all security-sensitive actions are audited. Verify coverage for account changes, profile changes, evidence ingestion/review, matching runs, collective membership changes, referral actions, workspace operations and administrative actions.

Check that:

  • Logs exclude passwords, access/refresh tokens, OTPs and secrets.
  • Audit records identify actor, action, target, time and relevant outcome without storing unnecessary sensitive content.
  • Audit data has appropriate access controls and retention.
  • Correlation IDs are returned consistently and allow request tracing.
  • Revocation/OTP/lockout state behaves correctly across worker processes and restarts.
  • Backup, restore and incident-response procedures are documented.

docs.title: 9. Security review checklist
docs.text:
• Fix or replace require_self_or_admin so it compares the target user ID with the authenticated user's ID, or restrict its use to contexts where another verified check performs that comparison.

docs.title: 1. Overview
docs.text: KNode uses SQLAlchemy models and a PostgreSQL database configured through DATABASE_URL. The database stores users, organisations, funders, opportunities, requirements, evidence sources and claims, matching runs and results, collectives, referrals, workspaces, reports, and audit events.

docs.title: 2. Connection and sessions
docs.text:
database.py calls load_dotenv(), reads DATABASE_URL, raises an error if it is absent, and normalises postgres:// and postgresql:// URLs to postgresql+psycopg2://. The SQLAlchemy engine uses pool_pre_ping=True and echo=False. SessionLocal uses autocommit=False and autoflush=False. get_db() yields a session and closes it in a finally block.

Example DSN (replace every placeholder locally):

postgresql://<DB_USER>:<DB_PASSWORD>@localhost:5432/<DB_NAME>

Closing a session does not automatically commit a transaction. Transaction boundaries differ by service; inspect repositories/transaction.py and relevant service/repository code, especially rollback behaviour after exceptions.

Tests use an in-memory SQLite database with sqlite:// and StaticPool, enable foreign keys, call Base.metadata.create_all, and provide a rollback transaction fixture.

docs.title: 3. Main entities
docs.text: Table / model Purpose and key relationships users User accounts, role, status and optional organisation/funder association. organisations Organisation identity, mission, focus areas, countries of operation, capabilities and verification metadata. funders Funder profile, funding interests, geography and typical grant range. funding_opportunities Opportunity details, funder/source identifiers, eligibility information, coalition policy, deadlines and status. opportunity_requirements Individual opportunity requirements and optional structured values/source association. sources Evidence provenance, source URL/type, retrieval/publication information, content/storage references and hash. extracted_claims Claims extracted from sources, evidence text, confidence, review status and reviewer metadata. match_runs Matching workflow lifecycle, requester/target references, run type, status, algorithm version and errors. matches Match identity, organisation/opportunity association, score, score breakdown, requirement assessments and explanation. match_partners Partner suggestions associated with matching results. collectives Collaboration group and opportunity context. collective_members Membership, participation and response state for collectives. funding_awards Award records used by funding/trend-related functionality. organisation_email_domains Organisation email-domain associations. ai_files AI/document file records; the polymorphic entity_type + entity_id association does not use a normal foreign key to every entity type. reports Stored report content, including JSON content. A public report router was not found in the inspected source. audit_events Audit event data. The ORM attribute event_metadata maps to the database column metadata. referrals Referral records targeting an organisation or collective. A check constraint requires exactly one target. workspaces Workspace associated with a collective. workspace_items Items within a workspace, with optional assignee/author relationships using SET NULL where configured.

docs.title: sources and extracted_claims
docs.text:
sources records source associations with organisations, funders, or opportunities and includes source name/URL/type, storage key, retrieval/publication metadata, content text and hash fields. Exact nullability and foreign-key rules should be verified against models and migrations.

extracted_claims stores claim type/value, evidence_text, confidence_score (observed Numeric(5,2)), review status (default PENDING), reviewer and review timestamp, source/organisation association and creation time. The matching assessment path accepts only claims with review_status == "CONFIRMED" and non-empty evidence text.

docs.title: match_runs and matches
docs.text:
match_runs stores run_id, optional requester/organisation/opportunity references, run type (opportunity matching, partner discovery, collective building), lifecycle status (PENDING, RUNNING, COMPLETED, FAILED), algorithm_version, start/completion timestamps, error details and creation time.

matches stores match_id, run and organisation references, optional opportunity, match type, nullable numeric score, score_breakdown JSON, requirement_assessments JSON, explanation and creation time. The response builder also reads missing-information fields, strengths/gaps, score status, evidence coverage, eligibility status, run status and algorithm version. It detects legacy placeholder records so a placeholder zero is not presented as a real score.

docs.title: Other constraints and relationships
docs.text:
• match_partners stores partner suggestions associated with matching results.
  • collectives and collective_members represent groups and their member participation. Membership uniqueness and response timestamps are constrained in the schema/migrations.
  • funding_awards supports award and trend-related data.
  • organisation_email_domains stores organisation-domain associations.
  • ai_files uses a polymorphic entity association rather than a foreign key covering every target type.
  • reports stores report content as JSON; the inspected code did not establish a public report router.
  • audit_events stores audit metadata; the Python attribute event_metadata maps to the SQL column metadata.
  • referrals has a check constraint requiring exactly one of organisation or collective target.
  • workspaces and workspace_items associate work items with collectives/workspaces; optional author/assignee references may use SET NULL.

docs.title: 5. Types, constraints and implementation notes
docs.text:
• A custom GUID/UUID type and UUID factory are defined in models/types.py; verify behaviour on both SQLite and PostgreSQL.
  • Several fields use SQLAlchemy generic JSON, not PostgreSQL JSONB. Identified JSON fields include focus_areas, capabilities, structured_value, score_breakdown, requirement_assessments, report_content, and audit metadata.
  • Many enums use native_enum=False.
  • DateTime fields are timezone-aware in the model declarations and may use Python/server defaults.
  • Grant and revenue values use Numeric(19,4); score/confidence values use their own declared precisions.
  • Constraints include external identifiers, collective membership uniqueness, referral target exclusivity, collective response timestamps and funding-award rules.
  • Do not infer the live schema solely from SQLAlchemy models. Inspect PostgreSQL catalogs and Alembic state before making production changes.

docs.title: 6. Alembic migrations
docs.text:
Migration files live under alembic/versions/; configuration is in alembic.ini and alembic/env.py. The history includes more than one initial-schema migration, a later no-op-looking initial migration, a merge revision, nullable match-score work, organisation-email-domain changes, collective/referral constraints, sector and coalition-policy changes. The noted latest migration is b4f783d2d110_add_coalition_policy_to_opportunities.py, which merges two branches. Verify current heads/history rather than assuming this is still the latest revision.

Run against the intended database only:

uv run alembic heads
uv run alembic history --verbose
uv run alembic current

Generate and apply migrations only after review:

uv run alembic revision --autogenerate -m "describe_schema_change"
uv run alembic upgrade head

A downgrade can be destructive; inspect the revision's downgrade() implementation before running:

uv run alembic downgrade -1

docs.title: Migration workflow
docs.text:
1. Update the SQLAlchemy model.
  2. Generate a candidate migration.
  3. Review the migration for nullability, defaults, constraints, indexes, data backfills and downgrade behaviour.
  4. Apply it to a disposable PostgreSQL database.
  5. Verify the resulting schema and existing data.
  6. Update Pydantic schemas and service logic.
  7. Add migration, repository and API tests.

Base.metadata.create_all() in the SQLite test setup is not a substitute for validating Alembic migrations. Keep model and migration history aligned and resolve multiple-head conditions deliberately.

docs.title: 1. Purpose and boundaries
docs.text:
The Matching Engine assesses how an organisation's stored capabilities and evidence align with the requirements of a funding opportunity. It supports requirement-level assessments, eligibility conditions, a deterministic score calculation, partner suggestions and collective-coverage summaries.

The result is an evidence-based aid, not a funding prediction, certification or guarantee of eligibility. Missing evidence must not automatically be interpreted as proof that an organisation fails a requirement. Partner suggestions do not establish availability or agreement to participate.

docs.title: 2. Main components
docs.text: Component Responsibility routers/matching.py HTTP interface for matching operations. services/matching_service.py Orchestrates matching requests and persistence. repositories/matching_repository.py Reads/writes match-related records. services/matching_engine/assessment.py Passage/provider protocol, retrieval inputs, status and quote validation. services/matching_engine/gemini_provider.py Gemini prompt, JSON response handling, retries and output checks. services/matching_engine/provider_factory.py Configures or disables the assessment provider. services/matching_engine/orchestrator.py Requirement loop, evidence filtering, scoring, eligibility and summary generation. services/matching_engine/eligibility.py, eligibility_rules.py Eligibility conditions and aggregate eligibility state. services/matching_engine/scoring.py Deterministic scoring and evidence-coverage calculation. services/matching_engine/contract.py Contract/status compatibility and output shapes. services/matching_engine/views.py Response views and partner suggestion logic. services/matching_engine/collective.py Aggregates requirement assessments across collective members. services/matching_batch_service.py, services/jobs/opportunity_matching.py Batch assessment and job entry point.

docs.title: 3. Inputs and evidence retrieval
docs.text:
The request identifiers come from schemas.matching.MatchCreateRequest. Requirements are loaded from opportunity_requirements, including requirement_text and optional structured values such as category, published_weight, and dedupe_key.

The inspected assessment path filters evidence claims to review_status == "CONFIRMED" and non-empty evidence_text. A Passage carries claim/source/organisation identifiers and text. The lexical retrieval step tokenises text, keeps shared alphanumeric tokens of at least three characters, and sends at most five passages to the provider.

The following capabilities were not found in this matching path and should not be documented as implemented without further code evidence:

  • Embedding generation.
  • Vector similarity retrieval.
  • Metadata-filtered hybrid keyword/vector retrieval.
  • Page-level document chunking and a vector index.
  • Vertex AI embeddings or pgvector-based matching retrieval.

The current candidate retrieval is lexical and limited; it may miss relevant evidence expressed with different wording. The quality and scope of retrieval should be evaluated before scaling.

docs.title: 4. Requirement assessment statuses
docs.text:
Status Meaning in the current contract MET Requirement assessed as fully met with an accepted, verified quote. PARTIALLY_MET Requirement assessed as partially met with an accepted, verified quote. NOT_MET The prompt instructs the provider to use this only for explicit contradiction, not merely missing evidence. UNKNOWN No relevant evidence, ambiguous output, unverified quote or insufficient certainty. NOT_CHECKED No provider is configured after relevant evidence is found; represents an assessment not performed. ERROR Provider failure or invalid output.

A legacy contract maps SUPPORTED to MET, PARTIALLY_SUPPORTED to PARTIALLY_MET, and UNVERIFIED to UNKNOWN. The Gemini provider accepts MET, PARTIALLY_MET, NOT_MET and UNKNOWN. If the provider returns NOT_CHECKED, the wrapper converts it to UNKNOWN; the prompt does not ask the model to return ERROR. Preserve the distinctions in the application contract and avoid silently turning errors or missing evidence into negative results.

docs.title: 5. AI assessment and grounding
docs.text:
GeminiAssessmentProvider treats requirements and evidence as untrusted. It requests JSON containing a status, passage label, quote and short reasoning. It removes email-like strings and marker sequences, uses response_mime_type=application/json and temperature 0, and retries with exponential backoff. Logs include prompt version, attempt count, status, elapsed time and failure class rather than raw evidence prompts.

The wrapper validates the response using Pydantic, checks that the cited passage label maps to a retrieved claim, and checks that the quote exists in the stored passage after whitespace/case normalisation. An unverified citation is downgraded to UNKNOWN.

A valid quote does not prove that the model interpreted the evidence correctly. Human-labelled evaluation cases are still required, including contradictions, irrelevant passages, partial support and prompt-injection content.

docs.title: 6. Eligibility logic
docs.text:
eligibility_rules.build_conditions() currently handles these condition types:

  • Deadline: if a deadline exists, compare it with current UTC time. A passed deadline is FAILED; otherwise it is SATISFIED.
  • Geography: if eligible geographies are supplied, compare case-insensitive values against organisation.countries_of_operation. An overlap is SATISFIED; no overlap becomes UNKNOWN in the current implementation.
  • Organisation type: if eligible organisation types are present, add an UNKNOWN condition. No mapping/evaluation logic is implemented in this path.

assess_eligibility():

  • Returns NOT_ASSESSED when no conditions exist.
  • Changes SATISFIED or FAILED without evidence references/rule IDs to UNKNOWN.
  • Returns INELIGIBLE if any effective condition failed.
  • Returns ERROR if any condition is an error and no failed condition took precedence.
  • Returns ELIGIBLE only when all conditions are satisfied.
  • Returns NEEDS_VERIFICATION for remaining mixed/unknown states.

This is a limited rule set, not a comprehensive grant-eligibility engine. Confirm the product-required eligibility rules before presenting the result as a definitive eligibility decision.

docs.title: 7. Scoring formula
docs.text:
The deterministic scoring module defines these default category weights:

Category Weight programme_strategic_alignment 0.25 programme_delivery_capability 0.25 experience_track_record 0.20 target_population_context 0.15 team_capacity 0.15

Status points are MET = 4, PARTIALLY_MET = 2, and NOT_MET = 0. The maximum is 4. Only these three statuses contribute to the score. An assessed status without evidence references is normalised to UNKNOWN.

When all requirements have positive published weights, those weights are normalised and used. If weights are absent or incomplete, default category weights are used and redistributed across applicable categories and requirements. Duplicate requirements are merged by dedupe_key or requirement ID; the first item is kept and conflicts produce warnings.

For assessed requirement i, with normalised weight wᵢ, status points pᵢ, and maximum points pmax = 4:

Score = 100 × [Σ(i ∈ A) wᵢ × (pᵢ / pmax)] / [Σ(i ∈ A) wᵢ]

Here, A is the set of requirements the scoring module considers assessed. The score is rounded to one decimal place using ROUND_HALF_UP.

Evidence coverage is:

Evidence Coverage = 100 × assessed weight / total applicable weight
  • COMPLETE: all applicable weight was assessed.
  • PROVISIONAL: some, but not all, applicable weight was assessed.
  • NOT_CALCULABLE: no applicable requirement contributed to a score.

This formula describes the code, not an approved product policy. Confirm with the product owner whether a numeric Match Score and sorted results are permitted before treating them as a user-facing decision signal. The explanation text states that the score represents capability alignment, not funding probability or proof of eligibility.

docs.title: 8. Partner discovery
docs.text:
The current view logic:

  1. Treats lead requirements in UNKNOWN, NOT_CHECKED, ERROR, NOT_MET, or PARTIALLY_MET as gaps.
  2. Finds candidate assessments with MET or PARTIALLY_MET for the same requirement.
  3. Emits a “may complement” label.
  4. Returns candidate claim/source IDs for the relevant requirement.
  5. Sets participation_confirmed to false and includes a disclaimer.
  6. Sorts suggestions by the number of requirements they may cover, then by name and ID.

This is not an AI-driven semantic partner search. It uses stored assessment rows and deterministic coverage comparisons. Inspect candidate generation and the bulk-assessment path for performance and data-scope behaviour before scaling.

docs.title: 9. Collective coverage
docs.text:
services/matching_engine/collective.py aggregates requirement assessments per organisation. It tracks contributors and deduplicated claim IDs for each requirement.

  • COVERED: at least one member has MET.
  • PARTIAL: the best contributing status is PARTIALLY_MET.
  • UNRESOLVED: no covered/partial result exists and unresolved member assessment states remain.
  • UNCOVERED: all relevant available assessments are negative without unresolved states.

The summary counts covered, partial, uncovered, unresolved, and unconfirmed participants. This helper is not itself a provider call. The separate services/coverage_service.py describes its workflow as deterministic and states that it does not write matches or update match_score.

The application also has two coverage routes identified in the API inventory: a versioned matching-service response and an unversioned deterministic coverage response. Verify that both are intentional and document their different contracts.

docs.title: 10. Persistence and response construction
docs.text:
The schema stores:

  • Workflow lifecycle in match_runs.
  • Match identity and assessment result in matches.
  • Partner suggestions in match_partners.
  • Requirement definitions in opportunity_requirements.
  • Evidence provenance in sources and extracted_claims.

The response builder reads score_breakdown, requirement_assessments, missing_information, strengths/gaps, score status, evidence coverage, eligibility status, run status and algorithm version. It detects legacy placeholder records and avoids presenting a placeholder zero as a real score.

Verify transaction boundaries, rollback behaviour and whether all related records are written atomically when a provider or database operation fails.

docs.text:
• Evaluate all eligibility rules required by the product.
  • Agree canonical assessment statuses and score policy with the product owner.
  • Add evidence freshness/version handling and stronger retrieval where justified.
  • Test quote grounding and contradiction cases against labelled examples.
  • Verify per-route authorization and cross-tenant access.
  • Verify PostgreSQL transaction behaviour.
  • Test duplicate request and idempotency behaviour.
  • Document whether each matching path is synchronous or batch-only.
  • Establish reliable production scheduling for batch jobs.
  • Test provider-disabled, missing-key, timeout, malformed JSON, retry, prompt-injection and cost-limit scenarios.
  • Measure retrieval quality, false positives/negatives, score stability and coverage semantics before making product claims.

See API Reference for endpoint contracts and Testing and Operations for the recommended test matrix.

docs.title: 1. Test suite overview
docs.text:
The inspected repository contains tests for API routes, services, repositories, authentication, matching, collectives, evidence, audit, AI, email and error handlers. The extracted tree contained 71 files matching the test*.py naming pattern. This is a file count, not a test-case count and not evidence that the tests pass.

Key test support files include:

  • tests/conftest.py
  • tests/factories.py
  • tests/helpers.py
  • Matching-specific test helpers and feature test modules.

docs.title: 2. Test database and fixtures
docs.text:
tests/conftest.py creates an in-memory SQLite engine, enables foreign keys, calls Base.metadata.create_all, and provides a rollback transaction fixture. API tests use FastAPI TestClient and override get_db. Authentication stores are cleared around tests.

SQLite fixtures are useful for fast unit/API tests, but do not prove PostgreSQL UUID, enum, JSON, migration DDL, locking, concurrent transactions or query behaviour. Maintain a separate disposable PostgreSQL integration-test workflow for migration and database-specific behaviour.

The sample module name is illustrative only; use an existing filename in the checkout.

docs.title: 4. Recommended coverage matrix
docs.text: Area Tests to verify or add Authentication Registration/login success and failure, email/login verification, expired/invalid tokens, refresh/logout, inactive users, lockout and OTP attempt limits. Authorization Cross-organisation reads/writes, cross-funder match reads, admin scope, body/query ID attacks, evidence access, collective membership and workspace access. API contract OpenAPI schema, response-model serialization, expected status codes, consistent error payloads and duplicate coverage route behaviour. Matching statuses MET, PARTIALLY_MET, NOT_MET, UNKNOWN, NOT_CHECKED, ERROR, and legacy status mapping. Evidence grounding Exact/sub-string quote, wrong claim ID, quote from another organisation, empty evidence and unconfirmed claim. Retrieval No overlap, ties/order, token normalisation, result limit and equivalent requirements phrased differently. Scoring No scorable requirements, unknown category, partial published weights, duplicate/conflicting dedupe keys, missing evidence references and rounding. docs.title: 9. Logging and operational verification
docs.text:
The application configures logging in main.py, installs correlation-ID middleware, and logs unhandled exceptions. The matching provider logs prompt version, attempt count, status, elapsed time and failure class rather than raw evidence prompts. The email service logs whether email was sent or skipped.

The following were not verified in the inspected source:

  • Metrics backend or distributed tracing exporter.
  • Alerting integration or production log aggregation.
  • Database performance dashboard.
  • Complete audit coverage for sensitive actions.
  • Dedicated readiness endpoint that verifies database/provider connectivity.

Do not treat /health as a readiness check for the database or external providers.

docs.title: 10. Deployment checklist
docs.text:
The repository includes Procfile and GitHub workflows named ci.yml, pr-checks.yml and deploy.yml. The README describes a Heroku workflow, but no deployed instance was inspected. Before release:

  1. Build from a clean dependency resolution.
  2. Configure secrets through the deployment platform's secret mechanism.
  3. Run Alembic migrations as a controlled release step.
  4. Verify the app process and start command.
  5. Confirm /health responds after deployment.
  6. Run smoke tests for authentication, organisation/opportunity access and matching.
  7. Schedule batch jobs only if intended; verify locks, retries and duplicate execution safety.
  8. Verify SMTP and AI credentials, network access, quotas and provider failure handling.
  9. Confirm backup/restore, log retention, monitoring and incident-response procedures.

docs.title: Add an endpoint
docs.text:
1. Find the existing router for the functional area.
  2. Follow the router's existing path-prefix convention.
  3. Add request/response schemas if existing contracts do not fit.
  4. Put business logic in the service layer.
  5. Add authentication and resource-level authorization explicitly.
  6. Add repository methods where they fit the persistence pattern.
  7. Test success, invalid input, missing resources and cross-tenant access.
  8. Confirm the route appears at the intended full path in /openapi.json.

docs.title: Change a database field
docs.text:
1. Update the SQLAlchemy model.
  2. Generate an Alembic migration.
  3. Review nullability, defaults, constraints, data migration and downgrade behaviour.
  4. Apply it to disposable PostgreSQL.
  5. Update schemas and service logic.
  6. Add persistence and API tests.
  7. Do not rely on Base.metadata.create_all() as a substitute for migration testing.

docs.title: Extend matching behaviour
docs.text:
1. Define status semantics and evidence requirements before changing logic.
  2. Keep pure logic in services/matching_engine/ where possible.
  3. Keep provider access behind AssessmentProvider so it can be mocked.
  4. Preserve claim IDs, source IDs, quotes and status notes.
  5. Validate provider output and verify quotes against cited passages.
  6. Keep eligibility separate from capability score calculation.
  7. Test missing/contradictory evidence, invalid output, provider failure, duplicate requirements and unknown categories.
  8. Add labelled evaluation cases before changing prompts, model configuration or retrieval.
  9. Record model/prompt/algorithm versions where the schema supports it.
  10. Verify access control before retrieving or returning partner and collective information.
